newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asia Grain-Japan waits for China corn price fall.
newsitem.headline: E.Asia Grain-Japan waits for China corn price fall.

text.p: After China's recent re-entry into the world corn market its prices have yet to fall low enough to tempt Japanese buyers, traders said on Monday, meanwhile firm Chicago futures have sidelined South Korean corn purchasers.
"We've received some sales offers for Chinese corn, but they're not cheap enought to shift from U.S. grain," a senior trader at a major Tokyo trade house said.
China, once one of the world's biggest corn exporters, banned overseas sales of the grain in December 1994 to help re-build dwindling central stocks.
But it recently re-entered the market selling corn to South Korea, the Philippines and Malaysia, traders said last week.
"Unless China cuts offer prices to below $130 a tonne (C&F), we can't find a strong reason to cancel U.S. corn," another trader said.
Traders said they were also reluctant to buy Chinese corn because of some defaults on shipments to Japan in late 1994.
"A shorter shipment period (against U.S. origin) is a benefit. But our bottom line is that it looks risky to depend on China heavily...," a senior official at a feed maker said.
Japanese buyers are currently purchasing U.S. origin corn for April-June shipment and have so far covered up to 30 percent of their requirements for this period, traders said.
Premiums for U.S. corn were quoted at between 94 and 96 U.S. cents a bushel over the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) May contract, traders said.
They said nearby freight rates from the U.S. Gulf to Japan for bulk grains were indicated at about $25.50 a tonne.

In South Korea, buyers are expected to hold back on their purchases this week after corn futures on the Chicago Board of Trade ended higher on Friday on a strong corn figure in the USDA's weekly export sales report.

Traders said the buyers are likely to take a break after purchasing at least 520,000 tonnes of corn last week. Since the middle of January South Korean firms have purchased 84,000 tonnes of Chinese corn.
"We have covered most of our needs for April arrival and will wait until prices fall to our target level," a trader with Cheiljedang Corp said.
But some traders said expectations for a weaker tone in corn futures later on Monday, helped by a bearish USDA cattle feed report, may tempt some companies back into the market.
"We expect corn prices to fall this week because of the bearish USDA cattle feed report," a trader with the National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF) said.
The number of cattle placed on feed during December, according to the USDA, was about 10 percent below expectations.
If corn prices fall this week, the Korea Feed Association may buy one 50,000-tonne cargo for arrival in April, one trading source said.

Meanwhile, South Korea's state-run Agricultural and Fishery Marketing Corp will tender to buy 40,000 tonnes of U.S. soybeans on Wednesday and the Korea Feed Association will tender 40,000 tonnes of soymeal and 5,000 tonnes of rapeseed meal on Tuesday.
One local soybean processer is also looking for 50,000 tonnes of U.S. soybeans this week for shipment in the first half of February from the U.S. Gulf, a soybean trader said.

The NLCF trader said dry bulk freight rates from the U.S. Pacific northwest to South Korea have fallen slightly to between $12.5 to $13 a tonne from $14 to $14.50 a week ago, while rates from the U.S. Gulf have eased to between $22.50 to $23 from $24
In Taiwan, buyers are expected in the market for up to 92,000 tonnes of soybeans and 16,000 tonnes of corn this week, local traders said on Monday.
They said domestic soybean buyers had returned to the market to cover their production needs as many expect to see higher world futures prices ahead.
In the Philippines, grain importers are expected to be in the market for wheat and corn in the coming week if prices dip to "reasonable" levels, government and trade officials said,

"Philippine flour millers may likely buy wheat for their March requirements if the price of dark northern spring and western white wheat in the United States fall from present levels," said an executive in one of the country's largest flour millers.
